Macaroni penguin (Eudyptes chrysolophus) eggs are incubated for a period that reflects the thermal constraints of the sub-Antarctic breeding environment. During incubation, the attending adults maintain a nest temperature that closely tracks their own core body temperature, typically around 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. At this incubation temperature, the chick develops within the egg and finally hatches after a developmental period of 36.5 days [ab = 36.5 days], although it must be noted that this incubation occurs at a slightly lower, more stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] within the egg's microclimate beneath the brood patch. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 101 grams [Wwb = approximately 101 grams], a modest mass that reflects the considerable yolk reserves already consumed during the later stages of embryogenesis. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, calculated as the mean of the A-egg and the slightly smaller B-egg, is recorded as 142 grams [Ww0 = 142 grams], revealing that the chick loses roughly 29% of the egg's original mass during the incubation and hatching process.

The early chick-rearing phase in Macaroni penguins proceeds under the same thermal regime maintained by the brooding adults. While the nestling is continuously brooded, the parent's body heat keeps the chick at a stable temperature close to 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], which is essential for efficient growth and development. Under these conditions, the fledgling stage is reached relatively quickly, with the young bird undertaking its first true flight and achieving nutritional independence from its parents after approximately 65 days [tx = approximately 65 days] at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] since birth. This relatively brief fledging period, compared to some other penguin species, reflects the intense, short sub-Antarctic summer during which prey is abundant and days are long. The chick undergoes a rapid transformation from a downy, brooded nestling into a fully-feathered juvenile capable of thermoregulation and independent foraging. This developmental trajectory, culminating in the fledgling independence stage, is finely tuned to the seasonal pulse of krill availability in the Southern Ocean, ensuring the young bird can fend for itself before the onset of winter.

Puberty and the onset of sexual maturation in Macaroni penguins are dependent upon achieving a critical body size, which is itself linked to the energetic conditions experienced as a juvenile and sub-adult. The time since birth at puberty, when the gonads first become active and the bird is physiologically capable of breeding, is approximately 195 days [tp = approximately 195 days] under typical conditions at a body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. However, while puberty occurs early in life, the first successful breeding event is considerably delayed. The age at first reproduction, marking the time since birth at first brood, is approximately 5 years [tR = approximately 5 years] for this species, a value that is comparable to that reported for the closely related Fiordland penguin (Eudyptes pachyrhynchu at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]s). This substantial gap between physiological puberty and actual first reproduction is a classic life-history feature of long-lived seabirds, reflecting the time needed to acquire foraging skills, secure a nesting territory, and establish a stable pair bond.

Adult body mass in Macaroni penguins exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females being significantly heavier than males. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the asymptotic adult body mass, is approximately 5210 grams [Wwi = approximately 5210 grams], whereas the corresponding value for males is lower at 4760 grams [Wwi = 4760 grams]. This pattern, with heavier females, is unusual among penguins and is thought to relate to the intense female-female competition for high-quality nesting sites within the dense, crowded colonies. The lighter male body mass may confer an advantage during the long foraging trips he undertakes to provision the incubating female and later the chick. These mass values represent the maximum recorded body mass in adults under optimal foraging conditions; body mass fluctuates considerably across the breeding season, with birds losing a substantial fraction of their body weight during extended fasts on land.

Longevity records for Macaroni penguins indicate a species with a moderately long lifespan for a seabird of its body size. The maximum lifespan observed in the wild, representing the oldest documented individual, is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], recorded during long-term mark-recapture studies at at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] South Georgia. This lifespan, measured under natural thermal conditions of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in a single, slow-growing offspring per breeding attempt. While their maximum reproductive rate, expressed through clutch size, is limited to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], only one of these eggs typically survives to produce a fledgling. Female Macaroni penguins typically produce just a single successful clutch each year [F_R_i = single successful clutch each year], a low frequency that is offset by the high adult survival rate and the many years of reproductive opportunity afforded by their long lifespan.
